As fate would have it... it was supposed to be our wine that the conductor in question last sampled, yet a Lupo claims that he had asked someone to deliver it.
And the vehicle that delivered the samples under suspicion happened to be the one that caused the accident involving the truck delivering our wine...
The AST's drivers have nothing to do with the poisoning!
Of course, I fully believe that. At least, I do, from a traffic perspective.
...Traffic perspective?
Regardless of whether the rider violated traffic laws, his actions objectively impacted the non-delivery of our goods.
He created a high-risk environment at a critical juncture, the result of which was that the contract was not fulfilled according to agreement.
So you're going after someone who did not commit any actual violations?
'Going after' is such a strong phrase. I said nothing of the sort.
We are simply assessing the associated liabilities in accordance with the law.
The Kuranta pauses, then continues.
The portions of damages that insurance does not cover must, of course, be borne by the liable parties.
Business is business, Commissioner Eirene. I beg your understanding.
Business?! This is highway robbery!
Ah, we regret that you see it as such.
I assure you, our company is most disappointed in this turn of events.
Meanwhile, we invite any interested drivers to pick up a pamphlet in hopes of future cooperation.
We continue to welcome rational choices.
W-Wait! Eirene! Say something! There's no way I can deal with what's on this piece of paper myself!
I guess I'll have to go to—
No!
Then what do you suggest I do? If you didn't sign that partnership agreement with these foreigners, that crash would never have happened, and Gianni wouldn't be lying in a hospital bed right now!
I know you just want to help us make money, but those Kazimierzians are going to sue me!
I've never even SEEN that much money my entire life! How am I supposed to pay it?
You said that regulations would protect the Truckers' Union, no, the AST's drivers once we were part of the municipal system!
I shouldn't have to deal with this on my own, right?
I know, I'll find a way...
Well, either you do that, or...
Or I go and talk to that Bellone associate behind you.
Eirene reflexively opens her mouth to say 'no', as she had done so many times whenever this subject is broached, but no words come out.
She sees a few drivers standing around the Kuranta in the distance, the same typical smile plastered over his face as always.

The man stands there, patiently holding a pamphlet, sometimes nodding and sometimes replying softly, looking more like a counselor listening to someone's troubles, than a salesman trying to advertise something.
The drivers listen to the Kuranta's explanations with perplexed expressions on their faces, while casting subtle, searching glances at Eirene.
Don't worry, I'll find a way... I will...
It has been a long time since Eirene last drove a truck to work. It has been a long time since she drove a truck on the new city's roads.
Parking spaces are always at a premium at the city hall, where the Agenzia per la Sicurezza dei Trasporti's offices are located.
Visitors from local businesses, guests from foreign trade associations, drivers of the AST, colleagues from other departments... vehicles of all shapes and sizes come and go.
There is no space for a truck.

In the afternoon, when Eirene is driving her truck out of the camp, she overhears the other drivers discussing the pamphlets that the Kazimierzian representative brought, some with excitement, others with suspicion.
They talk about the number of fines this quarter, the profits of each job, and their children potentially getting to work for a winery, a pharmacy, or a vehicle factory.
The pamphlets paint a picturesque future, not so different from what she saw when she chose the foreigners in order to reject the famiglie.
But she knows that they also represent other things.
Eirene continues to drive for a long time. As the colors of dusk fill the sky, she dials a certain number on her terminal.
Lavinia? It's me, Eirene... I'm coming over to the courthouse right now.
I need to talk to you. It's important.
What wonderful lighting. It complements your emerald eyes. Oh, how lucky I am to have a girl with such beautiful eyes.
You talk like I'm the one about to go on stage, Paola...
But yeah, you sure are lucky to have a daughter who can handle both performance and paperwork so brilliantly!
Hehe, yes, yes. So, my good daughter, I trust you'll handle tomorrow's meeting with the new shopping mall on the corner?
I have some new pieces brewing in my mind, and I'd like to put them to paper after the Red Wine Championship.
Of course, Paola. Leave it to me.
You should head to the stage now, your performance is about to begin.
Everyone will know of our Schwarzervorhang Orchestra after today's performance, and I'm sure you'll be busy.
Stage lights peek through the gap between the backstage curtains, outlining the Caprinae's horns as she raises her baton.
She saw only a silhouette.
Under the slanted cellar lamps, the reflections off the drinking glass faded and reappeared as the figure moved.
Liesel wanted to approach the figure; perhaps they were lost and in need of directions.
But she only took one step before the other turned in response and quickly moved past the shelves.
As the two brushed shoulders, the light revealed towering horns atop a black hood.
Horns...? A Caprinae's horns?
I'm sorry.
*cough*, *cough* *cough*...!
The blinding stage lights shine down on the floor where Paula fell, the spilled wine pooling glaringly like fresh blood.
Her mother's lips, which were smiling and praising her, are now dyed a shade of ominous wine red.
The bright lights cause Liesel's vision to blur, yet Paola's lifeless eyes fail to capture any of it.
Paola...?
Mama!
—Liesel?
Huh?
I was just saying, we'll handle the partnership and payment according to the contract.
I'm sure you understand?
Ah, sorry. I was distracted...
No worries. I understand, you're trying to keep the orchestra together after such a huge blow. It must be difficult.
*sigh* Again, I am so sorry for what happened to Frau Paola.
This city has lost a beautiful and talented artist!
I myself am grieving the tremendous loss, I can't imagine how her adopted daughter must feel.
I appreciate your sympathy...
I hope you bounce back quickly! I've prepared some condolence gifts for your group, you can share them later.
You shouldn't have. We are honored to simply be working with you.
So, about the performance fee...
Don't worry about it. We won't claw back the deposit.
But as I was about to say, we have decided to not continue our cooperation.
I hope your group can find solace and weather this difficult time.
W-Wait, you're not renewing the contract?!
Yes. Without a dazzling pearl like Frau Paola, your orchestra has lost its backbone. I fear the standard of your performances will not return to its original level anytime soon.
After all, we are a business, not a charity—Ah, sorry. Was that too blunt of me?
Then, what about our performances scheduled for the next two days—
Cancelled, of course. The original plan was to let our guests enjoy your music accompanying their wine tasting.
But now city hall has closed the theater for an investigation of this incident, so there's no way to continue the competition.
I'm suffering a terrible loss too, you know!
Then what about the fees for the previous performances? Our Red Wine Championship warm-up performances were perfectly fine—popular, even!
Our contract clearly states 'In the event that force majeure leads to the termination or cancellation of a performance, the client is not obliged to pay the corresponding fee.'
In other words, we pay the balance only after all the performances have been properly performed.
Ah, perhaps your grief caused you to forget this clause?
No, that is not...
*sigh* No one wanted for this to happen. It's a terrible loss for us as well, so I hope you and your orchestra can empathize.
If there's anything else we can help with, just let us know and we'll try our best to assist.
...I understand.
If you ever need our services in the future, just let me know.
Of course, of course.
But I must ask, will your group be alright, performing without Frau Paola?
Liesel! You're finally back!
Timpani pulls Liesel onto the sofa in the middle of the rehearsal room, then sits down next to her, awkwardly patting her shoulder.
His back is straight, but his bloodshot eyes betray his effort to remain chipper.
Man, that Czarek's a stubborn one. Didn't think he'd insist on discussing the contract with you just because your mother's signature was on it.
We already told him to come to us. You've just suffered such a tragic loss, how could he talk business with you right now?
Right! He has no clue how close you two were. You know, we can tell at a glance how long you spent sobbing last night!
Just stay put here, Liesel. Enough worrying over the past two days. Let us old timers handle the rest.
Just look at your hands, all wrinkly and calloused from doing the cleaning and chores all by yourself just to save money.
Huh? No, I'm fine...
Actually, I'd rather you all not worry yourselves over this. Just concentrate on rehearsal...
Right, so what did he say about our future performances? Same as usual, or are we doing something new?
But Paola didn't finish her new piece.
About that...
Our future performances... are all cancelled.
Czarek also says we only get the balance payment after all the performances are done, but now...
What?! That verdammt Kazimierzian Scheißkerl!
(Whispering) Hey, Timpani!
Trombone stops Timpani from continuing his onslaught of expletives with a tiny pinch, and gestures with her eyes for him to show some consideration to the girl on the sofa.
Ah, sorry, Liesel. I wasn't mad at you, don't worry.
Damn that Czarek, bullying a girl! Has he no heart? The Red Wine Championship ended just a while ago—you haven't even had a chance to recover, and he lays this on you?
Liesel, you should go to bed. You haven't gotten a wink of sleep since yesterday.
I left a cup of hot cystymilk in your room, so have some, alright—Oh no, it might be cold by now, why don't I go warm it up for you?
Liesel opens her mouth to answer, but nothing comes out as she notices everyone's red eyes and tired expressions.
She manages nothing, and ultimately shakes her head weakly, refusing Trombone's offer as she gets up to leave.
In the hallway outside the room, she leans against the wall, listening to the vague murmurs from inside.
*sigh* What do we do now?
Paola's gone, and so is our performance fee.
We were counting on this Championship to get our name out there and secure new gigs, but now it's going to be nearly impossible...
We need cash to rent our rehearsal space, for instrument maintenance, and food isn't free either.
Paola didn't have much saved. She shared whatever she had with us...
Let's pool what we have, I think we can manage another ten to fifteen days or so.
But who will conduct us now that Paola's gone? How are we going to perform without her?
How did she even...? That Bellone Lupo, why did he hurt our Paola?
It just makes no sense. What does his mafia have to do with us?
Maybe they thought she was in someone's way?
Or did we break one of their rules by taking gigs here?
Who knows?! The Siracusan gangsters are a ruthless bunch.
City hall says investigations are ongoing... but who knows if they'll actually go anywhere.
What can we even hope for? This city is still Siracusa, after all. I think they're just pretending to exercise the law.
Personally, I think we should never forget what the Bellones did to Paola.
If I ever see one of their mobsters, my fist is going straight in their jaw!
Don't be rash. If they could murder Paola just like that, I'm sure they could end our lives just as easily.
We all came from Leithanien. Could it be... they're after Leithanians...?
...Surely not...
If that's not it... I don't know how else to explain it...? Why would they go after a woman as great as Paola...?
I've had enough of the Siracusan mafia! Why don't we just leave for Victoria or somewhere even further? How's Columbia sound?
We might have to quit playing, but we can do odd jobs or whatever to feed ourselves, just like we did before we met Paola.
Hmm... we should take Liesel with us.
Of course. Even if I only earn enough for a bowl of macaroni, you bet half of it's going to the girl. She will not starve on my watch!
Liesel does not manage to make out what the rest say in response, nor does she have the will to listen further.
She only feels her head spinning, her eyes stinging, her entire body heavy like lead, she only wants... to fall into Paola's embrace.
*creak—*
Liesel does not return to her own bed, and instead opens the door to Paola's room.
Paola forgot to shut the window tight on the day of the Championship, and the rain from last night had soaked the nearby stack of music sheets. Even a day later, the paper remains wrinkled.
You forgot to close the window again, huh?
Even though I'd remind her every night. Honestly, everything else might as well be dust, once she dove into her music.
Paola...
The tears she tried her best to hold back for the sake of the meeting with the Kazimierizian businessman and the orchestra now burst forth once more.
Liesel gathers the sheets by the window, trying to smooth out the wrinkles on the paper, but even her fingers appear to her as blurry as the notes soaked by the rain.
She knows how dreadful and silly she must look. If Paola saw her like this, she'd join in the crying too.
Paola had been accompanying Liesel to her parents' graves when they overheard a lady performing a foreign melody nearby, and she cried the same way Liesel is crying now.
The trombone player was startled by the red-eyed Paola, but later became part of the family, just like Bassoon, and even Timpani—

Paola had been standing at the pier when she discovered Timpani driving piles into the ground with a steel drill. You have a good sense of rhythm, she said; so why not join my orchestra as a timpani player?
Liesel asked Paola before why someone as talented as her would leave Leithanien.
Paola only tilted her head in response then. She didn't fully understand herself—
Why didn't her countrymen understand that she only wanted to perform the pieces she liked—why couldn't they accept even that?
These scores... were her favorites...
The paint on this metronome's flaking off. She must have brought it from Leithanien.
Oh, so this earring was all the way in the back of this drawer. Paola was so sad when she thought she'd lost it.
This costume has been altered so many times, and it's still not finished. She said she'd wear it for the performance in two days...

Liesel gently picks up the crimson dress, her fingers tracing the gold thread on the neckline. The fabric is somewhat old with dye fading at its fraying edges, but the elaborate embroidery work is as brilliant as ever.
Next to the dress hanger is a staff, standing in silence.
Her staff... You had so much to teach me about Arts, so why...?
Why did someone do that to you?
The streetlights outside the window flicker to life, and passing headlights flash in and out of her vision, blurred by her overflowing tears.
Light. A flash of light.
The flash of light reflected off the drinking glass.
Liesel's fingers freeze. A blurry fragment surges forth from her memories like ice on a lake suddenly cracking from all the suppressed water—
The slender, hooded figure, half-hidden behind a shelf. The spotlight shining down, illuminating the glass in his hand.
Towering horns under the light.
That's... the man I thought was lost in the cellar...
But he's... a Caprinae...?
That's no Bellone, and no Lupo either, there's no way... What's going on?!
Like Trombone says, we have nothing to do with the mafia...
Could it be... Bellone really has nothing to do with this? Or maybe... he's not the murderer?
But, then why... why a Caprinae?
Liesel looks up, her gaze fixed on the photo on the headboard of Paola's bed.
A formal group photo of the Schwarzervorhang Orchestra after a performance. Other than a few Elafia, the other members, numbering a dozen or so, are all Caprinae.
Once she joked to Paola, asking if she intended to recruit every Leithanian in Siracusa into the group, and Paola laughed, saying it would be wonderful.
What if that person was no stranger, but one of... our players in disguise?
No, no way! How could I suspect one of our own?
But...
I have to find the killer... I have to know who killed Paola!
Paola, when you were teaching me Arts, you said telling the truth can sometimes hurt, but it's like a flame; warm and powerful.
You always told me to never lie, and to do the right thing...
But... what if doing it would scorch our family?
Liesel bites her lip, trying to stop herself from voicing her thoughts, but they only remain stuck in her head.
The exhaustion, shocks, pain, and fear from the past few days have squeezed her into a tiny ball, primed to blow.
Her tears no longer flow. She only feels cold.
Just a few more days until that murderer's been sentenced, and we'll bring Liesel with us and leave this place.
Tch.
What's wrong?
You see that luxury hotel over there?
Bah. Bellone businesses wherever we go.
Huh? You mean the priciest place, the one that's impossible to book is theirs too?!
Scheiße, they sure are raking in the cash.
Rich men like them probably can buy themselves an acquittal, right?
Gotta do every verdammt thing myself. Just you wait, I'll stab him a couple of times someday!
Enough. Did you forget what Trombone said? Besides, with that lame leg of yours, the cops would catch you right after you got your first stab in, and then you'd just break Liesel's heart again.
Right, right. We can't let her suffer anymore... no, I still can't just let it be!
Fine, why don't we go outside and spit on the ground?
Let's go!—No! That won't blow off enough steam. I need to get in a good punch or two.
Hah... You're the most stubborn man in this orchestra.
Fine! I'll come along—
What?!
Timpani and Bassoon have been detained?
For getting into a conflict on a Bellone property?!
No, I'm not Paola... No, nothing. Yes, I am Liesel Memminger. The phone number is correct.
Alright, I'll come at once...
She has barely managed to drift off when a shrill ringtone interrupts her sleep.
Liesel cannot decide if the caller's description of what happened or the resulting scene taking shape in her imagination is more devastating.
Her heart pounds violently as she puts on a coat before heading outside.
Perhaps because it is late at night, or maybe because a murder just happened, she fails to find a cab for hire. In a moment of desperation, she starts sprinting towards the nearest police station.

The night wind whispers to her like background noise leaking from an old stage. Liesel runs as fast as she can, even though her foggy thoughts only get noisier the more she tries to calm herself down.
Did they actually go looking for Bellone associates?
Did someone make a move?
Did they... do something for me... for Paola?
The wind stings her eyes, but she runs even faster, her balance nearly slipping.

lines.st: Personally, I think we should never forget what the Bellones did to Paola.

lines.x: No, there's no way...

lines.st: If I ever see one of their mobsters, my fist is going straight in their jaw!

lines.x: Timpani, Bassoon...
No... no! They wouldn't do such things!
Huff... *cough*, *cough*...
Liesel gasps for breath like a bellows about to burst as the night wind slips into her arms, sending her into shivers.
She notices a few passers-by ahead, looking at her as if they have spotted a lunatic.
She does not care, all she thinks is to go fast, faster—
But the closer she gets to the police station, the more the greyish-white building seems to slowly press down on her like a huge, unfeeling stage curtain.
Liesel slows down. She stands on the street corner, and spots an officer smoking outside at the gate in front of the lit-up station entrance.
For a second, she seems to want to turn and run.
Did they do this thinking they had no other choice, because I'm so useless?
What if they actually did something?
What if one of them is the real culprit?
What if I find the truth, and it's an answer the orchestra, or I, can't bear to hear?
She hates herself for doubting them.
She hates how her first reaction upon hearing 'Famiglia Bellone' and 'detained', was not to defend them, but to freeze as she recalled those towering horns.
Wh-What should I do...?
Paola...

lines.st: Daughter of mine, our orchestra wouldn't be what it is today without you. I'm so thankful.
Yes, I'll always be with you, and the rest of the orchestra needs you too.
Liesel, my girl, my pride and joy...
Someday, you will stand on the stage in my stead.
—No, not just for me. It has never been for me.
One day, you will become the best conductor in Nuova Volsinii, no, all of Siracusa.

lines.x: The wind seems to have stopped.
Liesel slowly but surely drags her heavy feet into the building.
S-So you're saying...
Timpani didn't hit you, and...
Struck these two Columbian businessmen instead?!
Ugh...
That's right.
Well, I got hit too, actually...
But hey, old man. You got a bum leg, but your arms pack a punch!
Damn straight! I'm a first-rate percussionist, you bet I'm good at hitting things!
If only that Columbian fatass didn't trip and eat your second jab, huh.
Ahem.
So here's the situation: We got a call about four troublemakers on the street, and then it turned into a fight between six.
After some questioning, we determined these two Columbian gentlemen in the Bellone Aldor Hall Hotel were fighting with mafio—uh, I mean with the hotel staff.
The staff had asked the Columbian men to step outside, but once they were on the street, the businessmen suddenly became violent.
Meanwhile, these two members of the Schwarzervorhang Orchestra tried to mediate the fight, but ended up involving themselves in the scuffle.
Yup, it's all that fatso's fault. He's drunk, and was harassing our receptionist—
H-Harassing?! Not at all!
I was just a paying guest in the hotel when suddenly I took a hit... Mark my words, I'm not done with you just yet!
Hah, haven't had enough?
You were the ones who stumbled into this lobby drunk, yelling 'Why should I line up?! Get me the biggest most mafia-style room!'
'Mafia-style?' What were you getting at, throwing words like that around a legitimate business establishment?
You scared off the guests who were trying to check in! You're acting like that's no big deal?
Exactly! Even from the entrance, we clearly saw how you scared the receptionist to tears!
(Whispering) Hey, zip it!
Bassoon pinches Timpani hard, who yelps and looks up to see Liesel's ashen expression.
Um, sorry, Liesel... You shouldn't have been called out here at this hour...
Um, all of us have you listed as our emergency contact... Paola told us to... so...
Ugh, it's my fault! I should've stopped him!
Liesel, say something... The silence is scaring me...
So the two of you... helped someone who didn't need your help in the first place?
Huh? Err... um, th-that seems to be the case, yeah...
Liesel is rendered speechless as she looks at both pairs of Bellone mobsters and Columbian businessmen.
In the middle, Timpani and Bassoon are huddling in fear like fowlbeasts caught in the rain, their pitiful gazes aimed at Liesel.
When was it...?
When was the last time I saw something so absurd...?
At the pier, faced with Paola's invitation, Timpani shook his head in confusion, and ignored the two to resume his hammering.
With his rhythmic hammering in the background, Liesel saw Paola suddenly straighten herself and her collar.
Foreman, sir. I'd like to resign on this gentleman's behalf.
From today onwards, he will no longer be able to hammer for you, for he shall join me in exploring the beautiful possibilities in the world of music.
Now then, arrivederci, my good foreman.
Huh?
—No, wait, what?!
Resign? Goodbye...? Who said he could go?
What, he can't?
O-Of course not! It's day labor, but he's not even done yet, and you want to take him away? It'll slow us down!
Oh! I see.
Is this enough, then? Go hire some other—go find another master artisan like Timpani here, and you won't fall behind schedule!
But...
The foreman was clearly shocked by Paola's actions. Her words stunned Timpani.
Behind Paola was Liesel, tugging on her mother's sleeve with an expression both amused and annoyed.
(Whispering) Paola, that's supposed to feed us for a whole week.
Huh? Really!
Everyone stayed awkwardly still for a moment, before the foreman quickly grabbed the florin from her, as if afraid she'd change her mind.
Hey, you over there, go find another worker for me—
The foreman turned to yell, and left the trio, depriving Timpani of a chance to respond.
...Huh?
*Sigh*.
I'm sorry, Liesel... maybe you should manage the money from now on.
And now—We three will busk on the street! I'm sure we can earn back enough for tonight's dinner!
The fiery sunset clouds from that day come back to life inside Liesel's mind.
The dumbfounded Timpani, the satisfied and smiling Paola, and her resigned self shaking her head were all bathed in a warm sunset glow, in the shade of a beautiful future.
...Pfft.
Wow, our whole family's so silly.
Paola, Timpani, Bassoon, Trombone, everyone... and even me. I'm the biggest fool of us all.
How could I have suspected my own family...? There's no way anyone would do anything like that.
It's alright, Liesel! I did what I did, and I'll pay the price. So don't worry your little head over this!
It's just a few days behind bars, probably. I'm used to skipping meals.
Can you start a beat, Timpani? Any rhythm is fine, just one you like.
What...?
Timpani's bold declaration to pay the price for his actions is interrupted by Liesel's sudden request.
He exchanges a glance with Bassoon, and even meets eyes with the Bellone mobsters and Columbian businessmen.
But the undeniable authority in her voice sends Timpani's hand involuntarily tapping on a metal bar.
With his rhythmic tapping in the background, Liesel straightens her back as well as her collar, looking toward the Columbian businessman.
Ahem! Allow me to introduce myself. I am Liesel, the leader of the Schwarzervorhang Orchestra.
We are the finest orchestra in all of Nuova Volsinii, which I'm sure you can tell from the excellent live performance by my timpani player, yes?
I should also mention we have a wonderful bassoon player in our midst, but I regret we do not have the equipment to offer a demonstration right now.
Alright, now that the introductions are out of the way—firstly, I would like to express my sincerest apologies for today's incident.
I cannot make decisions on their behalf, but I will take responsibility for my group. It is an undeniable fact one of my men hit you, and I am deeply sorry for it.
You are a businessman from faraway Columbia, yes? The high-end Piazza Parasota you've invested in is about to open in the city.
I think you chose the city for a good reason: its potential, order, and future cultural atmosphere.
Now, I'm not trying to excuse this unfortunate misunderstanding between your party and mine, but I'd like to offer something valuable in exchange for your forgiveness—a performance.
We, the Schwarzervorhang Orchestra, will provide a free and exclusive performance for the Piazza Parasota's opening ceremony.
E-Exclusive, you say?
Yes. Give us a time and we'll be there, performing a complete lineup of classical pieces of theater-grade quality—lighting and stage control included.
The conductor will be me, daughter of Paola Memminger. I will not fall short of her standards, for she personally trained me, and I am her pride.
Even if you are not satisfied with our performance, you will gain some buzz from the public either way, and won't take a loss, even if you decide not to hire us again.
But if you find us valuable—then I imagine you'd love to make Piazza Parasota the very first high-end shopping mall with a resident orchestra.
Of course, all this is to make one thing clear: This city only has a single orchestra worth investing in, and that's us.
Um, you know, boss... this sounds... pretty good?
It does seem like a good deal.
Hold up! How about figuring out who's actually in the wrong?
Well... this young lady has already taken the blame, so what else is there to discuss?
It's not like we meant to cause a ruckus...
Hmph.
Eek!
What do you gentlemen think?
Alright! You'll arrange everything that needs arranging, and we'll have your orchestra at the opening. However—
We are a high-end mall, after all... I do hope you won't disappoint.
Of course.
Next to the Columbian businessmen, Timpani and Bassoon are still as statues.
Only when the police officer waves them away do they both mutter something as if just jolted awake.
Liesel... you were the spitting image of Paola back there.
No, even more... uh, how do I put it? More Paola than Paola ever was!
I'm my Mama's daughter after all.
I'm Liesel Memminger of the Schwarzervorhang Orchestra.
In the dressing room backstage, Liesel is seated, surrounded by the joyful sound of her orchestra chatting.
Next to her is a stack of slightly yellowed scores—Paola's untitled quartet, with some edits noted in the corners.
Meanwhile, Paola's favorite composition has just won a standing ovation from the entire audience on the Columbians' magnificent stage.
Liesel runs her hand over the slightly faded ink, then stands up to face the orchestra.
Thank you all for staying.
I know... these past few days have been difficult, and stupid, but we held our concert, and we'll hold many more.
By Paola's will, in the name of the Schwarzervorhang Orchestra.
So, there is something I must tell you...
On the day of the incident, I saw Paola's murderer.
I'll find him somehow, and the law will punish him.
He... wasn't a Lupo—So probably not a Bellone.
It was a Caprinae I saw.
Grazie infinite, Signor Bellone!
I would've been at such a loss, had it not been for you and your famiglia.
Come now, Zio Elio. I didn't do anything.
Indeed, your name and presence were enough.
My landlord dropping by as you were visiting me was enough to make him reconsider collecting his rent on the spot.
After you left, he quickly agreed to give me two more weeks. That I'll figure out myself...
I don't understand, Zio Elio. Why are you...? What happened to your fruit stand?
Oh, that? Hah. Sold it long ago.
My little Emma had a fever this summer, and who would have thought it would leave her paralyzed?
Luckily, Demetri introduced me to a good doctor, said it was a serious yet common summer ailment for children, and she might lose her legs if it wasn't treated.
So I sold my fruit stand, and pooled cash from relatives to pay part of the doctor's fees. The rest is to be paid in installments.
She's out of the woods now, at least. She has a slight limp, but she's otherwise healthy. As for the rent and bills... I'll figure it out.
Your stand was on the corner... Metri and I bought oranges from you when we were little.
We've been neighbors for years. I could've lent you some money, and you wouldn't have had to—
No, no, Signor Bellone. It's a vast sum, I wouldn't dare accept such a favor from you.
Besides, your money wouldn't keep me afloat forever. I owe rent every week.
But now that I'm under Famiglia Bellone's protection... my landlord won't kick me out when I fail to pay; and even the bakery will sell me some food on credit.
But... you never wanted to join the Famiglia.
You always said there was no need for civilians to join or involve themselves in famiglie affairs—that the most important thing was to work hard and live your best life.
Ha! This old man was just naive.
A famiglia is more than fighting and killing. I finally understand that.
Don't worry, Signor Bellone. I may be old, but I know not to be ungrateful.
The Bellones have helped me, so if you ever need a favor in turn, just call me and I'll be there!
...You did this on purpose, didn't you? Metri.
I asked you the other day why I haven't seen his fruit stand, and you told me he went home for a relative's funeral.
You knew Emma was gravely ill.
And when you suddenly invited me here for pizza the other day... you knew Zio Elio would pass by and find me.
You handled it expertly, Leon.
Handled what? I played right into your hands, if I had known sooner—
—You couldn't have done anything about it anyway. You couldn't have possibly known what sort of hardship he would face. Your assistance would've been limited.
But at least I could've prevented him from joining the Famiglia against his wishes!
Only the Famiglia can help him now.
Is that so? I beg to differ. What did this facade cost him, and how long will it even last?
He should've had access to more work opportunities, while we—Siracusa—should guarantee them a livelihood through systemic measures. Relying on the famiglie won't address the root of the problem.
I hope the lesson you've learned from this is not charity or consideration for others, Leon.
You're the Underboss. Someday, you'll be the head of the Famiglia yourself.
A competent don knows offering timely help will earn you gratitude. They will owe you a favor, and repay their debt someday.
You sound so heartless, Metri. Why did you even bother introducing a doctor to Zio Elio, then?
Shouldn't you have let me do it, if you wanted me to learn to extract gratitude?
You didn't know how ill Emma really was, and you didn't know he would have no choice but to sell the fruit stand.
You just wanted to help him, and it had nothing to do with the Famiglia.
We... can only do as much as we can, no?
Besides, old Elio's oranges were always the best. He clearly knows how to pick his suppliers.
This is a trivial matter, compared to your available powers as the Mayor. Please, bring that murderous mafioso who ruined my Red Wine Championship to justice!
Signor Czarek, Demetri... Bellone's trial is this afternoon, but for now he remains only a suspect.
But who else could it have been? He sees me as a competitor and is not above dirty tricks.
I kept my wines safely stored in the cellar, and even arranged for professional security to guard them, only to somehow have them swapped with Saluzzo's!
The prime suspect was arrested at the party, yet only placed under house arrest.
And there have been plenty of people knocking on his door to visit, console, and even plot more nastiness!
The whole city thinks him innocent, while Saluzzo Vino is raking in record profits.
While I, poor old Radoslaw, have gained absolutely nothing after spending so much time and effort organizing an event here in the hopes of doing some business in this thriving new city!
As far as I know, The Red Wine has been publishing articles about this murder case, and this has brought a lot of attention to your event.

I understand you've already begun recruiting participants for your next Red Wine Championship, and there are even wine merchants from Columbia and Leithanien who have signaled an interest in participating.
Indeed, but I should be enjoying greater gains than just those. Now, I'm left trying to minimize my massive losses.
Signor Czarek, we pledge to run the city fairly, according to the New Urban Management Act, but our government will not serve the interests of a lone businessman.
Not you, or anyone else.
That so? I hear you grew up with that Bellone boy, and now he's even taken your family name.
I am no longer affiliated with Famiglia Bellone in any way.
But he's a member, no? Part of the purest Siracusan famiglia.
Even in his businessman costume, he's still most comfortable doing things mafia style.
...You need to present proper evidence before we can hold a formal trial.
Of course, we must follow due process. I am aware.
But my good Mayor, I pray you don't forget this—
Since the New Urban Management Act, many businessmen from Kazimierz, Leithanien, and Columbia have come here to trade.
And we, or at least the merchants under the K.G.C.C.'s banner, are only here in Nuova Volsinii and not in any other Siracusan city—because you have promised us the famiglie do not exist here.
The wine merchant leaves, but Leontuzzo remains still for a long time.
You seem exhausted. Did that wine merchant tie you up in his affairs again? Or is it Demetri?
*Sigh*.
He's convinced we won't have a fair trial, and keeps bringing up his chamber of commerce to pressure me.
Saluzzo Vino has indeed established itself in Nuova Volsinii under Demetri's management.
But it remains a local enterprise, and it's hard to judge if it can compare with the commercial capabilities of Czarek's Golden Prairie.
I fear Czarek is hounding Demetri not just because they're business competitors, or for that Championship incident.
Metri... is merely an opportunity for Czarek and the chamber of commerce backing him.
Most local merchants here do have ties to the famiglie, big or small.
And if this background becomes valid grounds for accusations of wrongdoing, the local industry will come under pressure...
But we do need those foreign capitalists to trade here.
We have to learn their modern ways of trade, we need their capital and goods.
Even the way they compete with each other is something we need. It'll make our local businesses iterate and evolve to keep up.
I'm aware of all that.
But, Lavinia... our current situation is so far from what we originally envisioned...
Yes, we planned for a city without the famiglie, run with fairness and justice, not favoring any particular party.
But now Nuova Volsinii has become an open gate to Siracusa, completely defenseless, free for any outsiders to enter, no matter their motives.
The first group is of course, the Kazimierzians who exploit the loopholes in the New Urban Management Act.
The exclusive shelf display agreement that Czarek and his fellow merchants include in their contracts has severely affected local industry.
The various logistics contracts with high fines have also driven our local truckers into a corner...
Yes, Eirene has informed me of their situation. It seems like the K.G.C.C. is trying to undermine our AST.
Also, other departments have given feedback on how they've been showing signs of wanting to involve themselves in the energy and healthcare sectors as well.
According to last month's reports from city hall, many businesses in the service industry have shuttered, while the manufacturing industry is also struggling.
Foreign-backed companies and shops have set up here, and they prefer to employ those from their own countries, so it is likely the job pool for locals will only shrink.
Despite our best efforts, prices are still trending upwards...
Our people are not doing so well.
And it is the Kazimierzians and Columbians we must face, but also—
The Leithanians who have come from all across Siracusa, and even from their own country with all manner of motives.
Yes. And before them...
The fairness and justice we seek remain necessary—I still believe in this.
But if such a pursuit must be traded for the livelihood of our citizens, then those so-called virtues will only end up being superficial formalities.
You're right.
I've... been mulling over it. Remember when I mentioned we might have to amend the New Urban Management Act—
We've made a revision. Want a look?
Leontuzzo takes the draft from Lavinia.
Two thin sheets of paper that should take no time to go through. But Leontuzzo flips through them multiple times before he finally looks up.
Impose tariffs on foreign goods...
Prevent foreign businesses from establishing a monopoly on key sectors like transportation, finance, and energy, and allow some factions with former famiglia ties access to lower management roles...
Issue franchise permits to famiglia-controlled corporations...
Is... this not a bit overboard? I fear people may say we're regressing to the old Siracusan way, or that we're favoring the famiglie.
I did propose change, but these amendments are difficult to accept.
I understand your concerns, Leon.
I know you, of all people, hope to keep the famiglie out of this city.
But you still seek to counter foreign capitalists with famiglie power.
Leon, we all know Nuova Volsinii's government and our authority over the city were granted at Signora Sicilia's pleasure.
But in Siracusa, as it stands now, the only force capable of uniting everyone is still the famiglie.
But what we can do is limit and prevent the famiglie from growing their power, ensure they do not succumb to infighting, and most importantly, keep them from infringing on civilian interests.
It's not an easy decision to make. Truth be told, I think it's not the right time to submit this draft either.
Most citizens enjoy the employment opportunities brought in by foreign companies, as well as their cheap and trendy imported goods.
Even if the K.G.C.C.'s ways inconvenience them, compared to the trouble caused by the mob wars of the past...
They will not think it much of a problem.
Silence spreads throughout the office.
Leontuzzo knows Lavinia is right. Because he used to harbor such plans in his mind.
But it is not so easy to make the decision.
I get what you're trying to say.
But just as Czarek and the K.G.C.C. want this chance to put Metri on trial, we also need an opportunity to convince ourselves and this entire city.
Yes, and this chance may well come soon.
The courtroom is packed. The afternoon trial has clearly drawn a lot of attention.
Sitting in the gallery are not only locals, but also the merchant Czarek's Kazimierzian partners, a Leithanian orchestra, and even Columbian traders.
All of their attention is fixated on one Demetri Bellone in the defendant's dock.

In accordance with the New Urban Management Act, the Nuova Volsinii criminal court will commence with the trial of the defendant, Demetri Bellone, on charges of the murder of Paola Memminger, case number 01452. Court is now in session.
I call Tommaso Esposito to the witness stand.
Signor Esposito, is it true you are a manager for Saluzzo Vino, in charge of the company's logistics?
Yes.
Two weeks ago, one day before the Golden Prairie's Red Wine Championship, you called an individual by the name of Sam at the Agenzia per la Sicurezza dei Trasporti.
You asked him to deliver two bottles of Saluzzo wine to the event venue.
Yes. I was very busy, and completely forgot about sending some wines to the competition, although I fortunately remembered to do so, the day before.
*sigh* Suffering from success, as it were.
When this Sam was delivering the goods via motorcycle, he came upon a crashed truck driven by an AST colleague, one Gianni. Gianni was on a Golden Prairie job at the time.
Coincidentally, Gian just happened to be delivering goods specially prepared by Golden Prairie for the competition finals, and you just happened to be there as well.
The coincidence isn't that unusual. Just goes to show how everyone loves doing things last-minute.
As for me, I was making my way over to the event venue to ensure my boss's instructions were being carried out properly, so I tagged along.
At the scene of the accident, you helped Sam get Gian into the ambulance, and you helped handle the aftermath—
Notably, you took those Saluzzo wines and placed them into the Golden Prairie box meant for the competition.
The Golden Prairie guys said they'd find another driver, so I thought I'd save myself some trouble, since we were both delivering goods to the same destination.
But you took the Golden Prairie wines out of their box.
And so the wines that appeared to the judges under the Golden Prairie name were, in fact, from Saluzzo Vino.
That's their own carelessness!
They only had to look at the labels on the bottles to avoid that mistake. Am I wrong, Your Honor?
...No further questions.
I call Letizia Maroni to the witness stand.
Signora Maroni, you work at the Nuova Volsiniese Police Academy as a toxicology expert and forensic pathologist.
You were responsible for the autopsy of the victim, Paola Memminger, as well as the testing of the utensils and wine in the case.
Yes.
Please inform the court of your findings.
Yes, Your Honor.
The autopsy results show Paola Memminger died of cyanide poisoning.
Traces of cyanide were found on the wine glass she used, but not inside the Saluzzo wine bottle.
In other words, the murderer applied cyanide only to the glass, rather than the Saluzzo wine itself.
I can only say the current evidence supports that conclusion.
Calling Liesel Memminger to the witness stand.
The little Caprinae steps out from the crowd of musicians around her, and slowly but resolutely walks toward the witness stand.
Signorina Memminger, is it true you are a member of the Schwarzervorhang Orchestra, and the adopted daughter of the deceased Paola Memminger?
Yes.
On the day of the Red Wine Championship, you went to the cellar where all the competition wines were stored for an inspection.
Yes.
While you were there, you brushed past someone who was neither a security guard nor a member of any participating winery.
...Yes.
Did you see what this individual did in the cellar?
I... saw him picking up a glass. But at the time, I only thought it a random, strange occurrence.
No problems arose after he entered the cellar, so I assumed he was just a lost spectator.
If I had known... If I had known what he was doing, I would have stopped him, and Paola wouldn't have...
Liesel's voice trembles slightly as her volume lowers gradually. She looks down, hunched over, but ultimately she straightens her back.
My condolences.
Did you get a clear look at his face?
...I only saw him for a moment. I saw his face, but couldn't make it out clearly.
Do you think you might recognize him?
No. He dressed very plainly. Thinking back, I believe he was maybe trying to trick the security guards, impersonating one of our orchestra members.
I don't know who he was, but there is one thing I do know... he was definitely no Perro or Lupo you'd typically find in Siracusa.
He had enormous Caprinae horns.
Murmurs rise in the courtroom, like ripples from throwing a stone into water.
Lavinia continues her questions, and Liesel recounts in detail what her orchestra members were doing at the time, establishing their alibis.
But no one cares for her words at this point.
So Bellone didn't do it. I've been thinking it made no sense.
He already won the championship, after all. What would he get by killing the conductor?
But what if there's something else we still don't know?
Also, couldn't he have just simply hired a Caprinae to do the deed?
His men have sabotaged our wineries. He's been obviously after us, disrupting our perfectly legitimate business operations!
Silence! Order in the court!
I call Elio Fabri to the witness stand.
Leontuzzo is shocked to see his old acquaintance in court.
He does not know why old Elio would be here.
He was not even aware that Elio had come to Nuova Volsinii.
Signor Fabri, is it true you are an employee of Saluzzo Vino, and responsible for procuring grapes for the company's production line?
Yes, Your Honor.
Three weeks ago, you reached out to Verdi Winery to discuss procuring raw materials for Saluzzo Vino.
Even though Verdi Winery's business has been declining ever since the Kazimierzian wineries set up shop, they always have the most aromatic grapes.
Our company has a long-term cooperative agreement with Verdi to purchase any surplus materials their production lines cannot handle.
The discussion was just part of my regular job.
But during this meeting, you learned that Golden Prairie was about to buy out Verdi Winery.
...Yes.
And so you conspired with Niccolo, a Verdi employee, to sabotage the winery's production facilities.
Furthermore, you also sabotaged their water supply and drainage systems, causing Golden Prairie to incur substantial maintenance costs after their acquisition.
...Yes.
You must be aware that these actions constitute unfair competition, and violate the New Urban Management Act.
What was your motive? Did the owner of Saluzzo Vino, Demetri Bellone, compel you to do this?
Did he intend to disrupt Golden Prairie's business operations?
Elio does not answer immediately.
The Kazimierzian businessman in the gallery is silent, his expression now relaxed.
Meanwhile, Leontuzzo fails to make out Demetri's reaction from his calm demeanor in the defendant's dock.
No one compelled me to do anything, Your Honor.
Everything I did was on my own conscience, out of my concern as a Nuova Volsiniese, as a Siracusan.
It's true Golden Prairie is a competitor of ours. And our rivalry means I know well the methods they use.
They dump their goods here for cheap, pressuring our local wineries into a smaller corner of the market, and then acquire them when they turn unsustainable.
But they don't run the businesses properly after buying them out, much less try to preserve their unique winemaking traditions.
They fire all the old staff to increase profit and efficiency, pretend to operate normally for a while, then shut it all down, leaving the vines to waste away.
Verdi's the fourth. Before them, it was Triptych, Passadi Hills, and Drizzle...
All those wineries suffered the same treatment.
That's how Kazimierz works.
They don't care about the effort we put into tending our grapes, nor for our lives and the memories carried by the unique astringency in our traditional wines.
All they want is to clear out their weaker competitors, one by one, until they monopolize all the shelves of every store.
And we'll ultimately lose any choice in the products we buy. When that happens, I doubt their prices will stay as low as they are now.
Well said. But that does not justify your use of illegal means.
I know.
I know what I've done won't stop the Kazimierzians from trampling all over our wine and other industries.
But I had to do something. I'll accept whatever punishment I deserve.
Murmurs from the gallery only grow louder and louder.
Lavinia raises the gavel in her hand, but hesitates for a while before she puts it down without striking the block.
Your Honor, if you would allow me a few words.
...Speak.
I believe the testimonies you've heard from the witnesses you summoned are sufficient to prove I have no connection to the murder of Paola Memminger.
But Elio Fabri is indeed in my company's employ.
I did not compel him myself, and he did engage in activities deemed illegal by the New Urban Management Act, targeting Golden Prairie.
I believe his reasons for doing so are perfectly understandable, not just to me, but to every Nuova Volsiniese sitting in the gallery right now.
But a violation of the rules is a violation. I do not expect the court to make an exception for him.
Though, as his boss, I am willing to bear the punishment for his crime, be it a fine or a prison sentence.
The murmurs are now so loud that even the gavel fails to silence the crowd. Reporters in the back rows leave to contact their newspapers.
Lavinia announces the end of the trial; declaring the verdict to be given at a later date following jury deliberations.
Amidst the chaos, Leontuzzo catches Demetri looking at him.
He watches as Demetri raises his hand, puts his index and middle fingers together, and gently points them towards Leontuzzo, then himself.
He recognizes the action—a unique gesture they have both used since they were little to signal 'catch you later for a chat'.
Leontuzzo does not respond.
Yes, we've confirmed with the team responsible for guarding the Bellone estate that Elio Fabri did not visit Demetri Bellone's residence following the murder of Paola Memminger.
We have not monitored any calls between them either.
...In other words, he just spoke of his own accord at the courthouse.
That seems to be the case, as far as we can tell.
The jury has yet to reach a verdict, so we can only continue to watch the Bellone estate and keep Signor Fabri in custody for now.
I'd like to speak with him in private.
By all means.
...Zio Elio.
I didn't know you were in Nuova Volsinii.
Oh? I thought Signor Mayor and Judge Lavinia would've come across my name while scrutinizing entry applications from Bellone associates.
I... didn't notice... but why are you still with them? I thought...
After Padre's death, Famiglia Bellone lost all the power it had. You should've left then—I know you never liked having to do things the mafioso way.
Leave? I lost my fruit stand, Emma's fever left her with a lifelong need for medication, and I've been struggling...
If Don Demetri hadn't invited me to join his winery and source grapes for him, I don't know how I would've survived!
Nuova Volsinii provides job opportunities for everyone with the will to shape a future with their own hands...
Is that so? Do you think small businesses can still survive, under the Kazimierzian merchants' heel?
But your acts of sabotage... the famiglie used to do the same.
The famiglie's ways of doing things... yes, they remind us, every citizen here, of our painful past.
I do admit it was a shameful act—but fortunately, Judge Lavinia allowed me an opportunity to speak the truth in court.
...Lavinia... was the one who arranged for you to be there?
Yes.
Sometimes, we have no choice but to only do as much as we can, no?
You asked me why I was still working for Don Demetri.
It is because he still adheres to the old famiglia creed—
A pack of whelps grouping up to help each other can keep all of us from being devoured by a bigger beast.
I heard your inauguration speech too. I could feel your passion.
You asked how our neighboring nations would view us? Would they see us as a new possibility?
But now, I believe they do. They see us as a new avenue, to exploit us for their own gain!
Yes, I work for the Don.
But is it the Bellone businesses I care for and want to protect?
No, it is our own industry! It is Don Demetri who gave us this opportunity to unite and stand against the great merchants!
Congratulations on your not guilty verdict, Signor Bellone!
Oh? I thought you, of all people, would be most eager to see me behind bars.
Just a misunderstanding!
The trial at court clearly proved your innocence, and the entire city knows of your magnanimity.
Let's put all the twists and turns that happened during the championship behind us. It is undeniable that your winery took the crown.
Saluzzo Vino now holds the title of number one winery in all Nuova Volsinii! Truly an enviable feat!
Thanks to you as well.
...Bah.
Surely you'll join the next iteration as well? Defending the crown would be a legendary achievement!
Perhaps.
But as you say, Saluzzo Vino is now the number one winery in the city—
So I'm afraid I no longer see the value in joining a so-called competition to increase the value of my products. Am I right?
...Fair enough. But Elio Fabri damaging a winery's water systems under the ownership of Golden Prairie surely impacts you somehow.
You said you'd pay his fine, or even serve his time. A noble gesture, but you don't necessarily have to follow through.
A trivial matter like that isn't worth a public prosecution in the first place. No one would've noticed the incident, had I not filed a lawsuit in the first place.
Signor Czarek, you can get straight to your point.
What is your goal here? I don't think it's just to repair our working relationship with a tiny favor.
Heh, I do appreciate frankness.
Regardless of our backgrounds, we are both businessmen now, are we not? So, Signor Bellone, I'd like to discuss a deal with you—
Let Golden Prairie invest in Saluzzo Vino. Our strong alliance will surely sweep the Siracusan markets.
And if, or when the time comes, our business empire will eventually expand beyond Siracusa and Kazimierz!
Oh, is that so?
Indeed! I know you currently do not lack for capital or production tech, and you have your reputation here.
But you must be aware of the Kazimierz General Chamber of Commerce behind me.
If we work together, our resources, like our comprehensive supply and logistic channels, and even the media channels we have ties with...
All of that will be available to you.
Surely a young, upstanding man like yourself doesn't want to stop at a single winery that doesn't even bear your name?
Have you never considered establishing a 'Bellone'—no, a 'Demetri' commercial empire?
Intriguing.
I didn't expect the trial's outcome to impact your company and judgement so much.
It did indeed leave its mark on my wine business, but Golden Prairie still retains its price advantage—
I'm thinking the K.G.C.C. was the impetus behind this effort to discuss a cooperative relationship.
We are businessmen, Signor Bellone. We are naturally driven by the pursuit of maximum profit.
It is normal for us to set aside our preferences when discussing a deal in our quest for the most beneficial result.
As your employee said, this is how Kazimierz works.
So, think about it, young man. Don't be in such a rush to refuse me.
Refuse? Did you think I would do that?
Leontuzzo arrives at Demetri's residence late at night.
The rain that lasted all day is now reduced to a faint drizzle, gradually slowing to a stop.
But his mood remains melancholic.
Security guards from city hall who are still at the estate lead him inside.
He thought Demetri would have come out to meet him, but he is mistaken.
Demetri is simply seated in a chair—a seat decided by old famiglia custom to be the don's—silently watching him.
A dim light over his head obscures his expression.
Leontuzzo suddenly realizes it has been a long time since he's read any expression from Demetri's face.
Here you are, after all.
...Yes. You asked me to come. I remember the gesture.
A glass for each of us? I can mix a ginger fizz with apple juice you like as a base.
Though it's hard to find traditionally pressed apple juice in Nuova Volsinii these days. I'm sure it's been a while since you've had any?
Fortunately, I found someone to help me acquire it.
I'm sure you didn't call me here to reminisce about the old days.
You can lower your guard.
When I arrived here, I think I spotted a Kazimierzian's car leaving.
The boss of Golden Prairie.
Czarek? What was he doing here?
He wants to work with Saluzzo Vino.
I agreed.
Why?!
Why? Is this not what you people at city hall want?
Bringing in foreign capital will help local businesses to thrive and evolve. This is how businesses here and even across Siracusa will gain access to a wider market.
Czarek was here as an agent of the K.G.C.C., and they offered generous terms. I had no reason to refuse.
...Kazimierzian businessmen aren't as nice as you might think.
You're worried for me.
You managed to gain the Saluzzos' assets with your particular methods, but this doesn't mean you will see the same results with the Kazimierzians.
We can only try and see.
Also, city hall will surely protect the interests of us local businesses, yes?
I know an amendment to the New Urban Management Act sits on your desk. Just missing your signature.
How do you...?
Just some of those so-called underhanded famiglia methods.
We should always seek all the intelligence we can to make the most beneficial decisions.
I believe I taught you this long ago when I was grooming you to be the don.
That amendment... is just a draft.
I might not even sign it.
You're hesitating, I know. You just can't make up your mind.
You fear the people will denounce you, that all your achievements will go to waste, that Nuova Volsinii will return to the old famiglia ways.
Should I not be afraid? It's too easy, going back to our familiar methods, while new sparks are so hard to start.
All the famiglie outside the city are watching our every move.
Give them one chance, and we'll be torn to shreds, never to recover.
But you have more to worry about than just the famiglie.
Besides the Kazimierzan and Columbian businessmen who exploit loopholes in the Act, there are also Leithanians trying to expand their influence in the city—
Did you know? I received some surprising news just before the competition.
Someone was dispatched here from the Leithanian border for the sole purpose of dispatching the exiled dissident Paola Memminger.
Leithanien's Eternal Grace forbids anyone from deviating from their Movement, even outside Leithanian territory.
And you used this to your advantage.
I didn't fan the flames, I simply let it be.
Fortunately, things turned out well, and you also have a chance to amend the Act.
Is this not what city hall has been waiting for, this whole time?
I believe Lavinia arranged that trial just for that.
I do intend to limit foreign capital here, but that does not mean—
Who else can you even rely on, if not us local businessmen?
Regardless of whether or not we have famiglia backgrounds, we are all at least complying with your city's rules.
We can act as your insurance.
Empty promises mean nothing to me.
I know you are skeptical of the famiglie.
But you should understand we started off as nothing but a band of whelps, powerless against the barrens and chaos of Siracusa.
We helped those around us, and hoped the day might come when we could win something in return, to improve our lives.
We Siracusans take care of our own. It is our tradition, and what I've always done.
So after the Don's death, after you left, I took the Bellones' reins.
Because I cannot let the famiglia lose their home.
Just as you cannot let the Siracusans lose ground to foreigners from Kazimierz, Leithanien, and Columbia.
Or am I wrong?
You will do great things, Leon.
One day you will actually be able to realize your dreams in Siracusa. I've always believed this.
I've heard this from you before... Metri.
I said back then you could be my right-hand man. The offer remains, even now, at city hall...
No, grazie. I really don't get along with Lavinia.
And, as you said before, there are things better suited for her, and others only I can handle.
Just like right now, some matters are for city hall to carry out, while others are better for us to do.
Your ideals alone cannot keep Nuova Volsinii alive. This city needs and must have the support of the old famiglie.
You sound so certain...
You met Signora Sicilia.
I'm sure you know well just how happy she is to meet young people with ideas.
Your established rules will keep the famiglie in Nuova Volsinii from running amok, while my ways will gather all the power and spirit of Siracusa.
This will become a new Guns and Order for this city, Leontuzzo.
As Leontuzzo leaves, Demetri extends a hand towards him.
A signal of cooperation. Leontuzzo hesitates for a moment before stretching out a hand himself.
They used to be close, no strangers to sharing hugs or laughter, but this formal handshake now is the first between them.
At the conclusion of their handshake, Demetri returns to his chair.
Then, just like Leontuzzo's father and every Siracusan don, he disappears into the darkness.
The rain is no more. The sky is surprisingly clear and tranquil.
That amendment... are you really okay with it, Lavinia?
We used to want for a Siracusa without even a trace of the famiglie.
I spent more than a decade under the Bellones' shadow, Leon.
I don't mind waiting a little longer.
Then the same goes for me.
